text:
Predicates:
SpillsFood(x) ::: x spills a lot of food on clothing.
Tidy(x) ::: x is notably tidy.
ClumsyFoodie(x) ::: x is a clumsy foodie.
GoesOutFrequent(x) ::: x goes out frequently to find new food restaurants.
Cleanly(x) ::: x is cleanly.
ValueOrderAndSpotlessness(x) ::: x values order and spotlessness.
PrioritizesFamily(x, y) ::: family y prioritizes order and spotlessness.
Family(x, y) ::: x's family y.
Premises:
∀x (SpillsFood(x) → ¬Tidy(x)) ::: If people spill a lot of food on clothing, then they are not notably tidy.
∀x (ClumsyFoodie(x) ∧ GoesOutFrequent(x) → SpillsFood(x)) ::: Clumsy foodies who go out frequently spill a lot of food.
∀x (Cleanly(x) → Tidy(x)) ::: If people are cleanly, then they are notably tidy.
∀x (ValueOrderAndSpotlessness(x) → Cleanly(x)) ::: If people value order and spotlessness, then they are cleanly.
∀x ∀y (PrioritizesFamily(x, y) ∧ Family(y) → ValueOrderAndSpotlessness(x)) ::: All people whose families prioritize order and spotlessness value order and spotlessness.
Peter is either a person who spills a lot of food on his clothing and is cleanly, or a person who does not spill a lot of food on his clothing and is not cleanly. ::: (SpillsFood(peter) ∧ Cleanly(peter)) ∨ (¬SpillsFood(peter) ∧ ¬Cleanly(peter))
Conclusion:
( (ClumsyFoodie(peter) ∧ GoesOutFrequent(peter) ∧ FamilyPrioritizesOrderAndSpotlessness(peter)) ∨ (¬ClumsyFoodie(peter) ∧ ¬FamilyPrioritizesOrderAndSpotlessness(peter)) )
